opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was a bit of a strange experience. Once the framework was actually usable, once the scaffolding, the tool calls, and the long-horizon loop were stable, I assumed I could plug in other models and get roughly similar results. That's not quite what happened.

Many models looked fine on short tasks. Ask them to write a function or fix a bug, and they do it well. The difference showed up when the task stretched over dozens or hundreds of steps. Some models would slowly drift. They'd forget why they had made an earlier decision, or they'd "succeed" by quietly changing the goal so it was easier to satisfy. Others were very capable but too eager: they'd take an action before really understanding the state of the environment.

What I came to appreciate is that "usable" isn't one property. A model has to stay coherent over a long context, recover from its own mistakes, and know when it doesn't know something and should go check. Benchmarks don't really capture that combination. You only feel it when you're running a real system and watching the traces.

It also changed how I think about our own work. It made me realize that the gap between models is no longer mostly about raw knowledge or single-turn reasoning. It's about agentic behavior: persistence, honesty about uncertainty, taste in how to decompose a problem. Those are things you have to deliberately train for, and you need environments that reward them. So in a way, using other models was the most useful part. It showed me very concretely where the frontier actually is, and what we need to build toward.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the contrast was pretty striking. Once Opus 4.6 had gotten the framework to a state where it actually ran end to end, I thought the hard part was done, and that swapping in other models for the day-to-day work would be straightforward. It wasn't.

What I noticed is that the framework carried a lot of implicit structure that Opus had set up — the way modules were separated, the conventions for how errors propagated, where configuration lived. Opus understood that structure because it had built it. When I brought in other models to extend it, they would often do something locally reasonable that violated one of those conventions. Not wrong, exactly, but inconsistent. And those inconsistencies accumulate. After a week I'd have three different ways of handling the same kind of failure.

The other thing was how they handled ambiguity. If I gave an underspecified instruction, Opus tended to go look at how the rest of the codebase did things and infer what I meant. Some of the other models would just pick an interpretation and run with it, and I'd find out two hours later that we'd diverged. So I ended up spending more time writing very explicit specs, which partly defeats the purpose.

That said, I don't want to be unfair. For narrow, well-bounded tasks — write a parser for this format, add tests for this function — the cheaper models were fine, and much faster and cheaper. So what I converged on was a kind of division of labor: use Opus for anything that touches architecture or requires judgment about the whole system, and use smaller models for the mechanical pieces where the spec is clear. The mistake I made early on was assuming that once the framework was usable, "usable" meant any model could work in it productively. Really it meant that a model with Opus's level of context-tracking could.

astra-6.text: Once the framework was usable, it was much easier to try other models because I had a concrete starting point. I could ask them to work within that structure and see whether their changes actually helped. That felt quite different from asking a model to figure out the whole framework from scratch.
